newsitem.title: GERMANY: Merger heralds shift in German banking landscape.
newsitem.headline: Merger heralds shift in German banking landscape.

text.p: Germany's overcrowded banking sector took a big step towards consolidation on Wednesday as a major merger began to take shape, reinforcing analysts' views that more are bound to follow.

State-owned Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG and regional bank Norddeutsche Landesbank said they were in merger talks which could create one of the country's largest banking groups with assets of more than 500 million marks ($293.2 million).
"This has given the process of concentration in the banking sector fresh nourishment," said Martin Haug, banking analyst at BfG-Bank in Frankfurt. "Stock market speculation of mergers will persist."
The combined bank would be larger than WestLB, the biggest publicly-owned regional bank, and would topple Commerzbank AG from its position as third-largest listed bank.
Only Deutsche Bank AG and Dresdner Bank AG would be bigger.

Bankgesellschaft and NordLB said a working party of management and their federal state owners had proposed integrating NordLB into a group led by Bankgesellschaft as early as mid-1998. Talks are due to be completed by the end of this year.
The two banks have been exploring possibilities for a link-up since last year but analysts said talks had progressed more quickly than expected.
"It's surprising that the news came so quickly," said one analyst at a German bank who declined to be named.
"The advantages lie principally in the increased size which will allow them to expand their investment banking business more than they could have done on their own."

German banking shares have scored huge gains since Deutsche Bank sparked takeover speculation last July by announcing it had amassed a 5.21 percent stake in Munich-based rival Bayerische Vereinsbank AG.
Germany's biggest bank said at the time it had no immediate plans to increase the stake and that the purchase was aimed at deterring rivals from launching bids.
Senior bankers have tried to quash the market talk and said public sector banks and cooperative banks were far more likely to merge soon than the big private sector players.

Analysts agree and detect a determination among the main retail banks to continue going it alone at present. They are all restructuring furiously to cut costs and win new clients, for example by setting up telephone banking subsidiaries.
But the rationale behind mergers even in the private sector is clear and many analysts believe the top five banks will have amalgamated to become the top three by the year 2000.
Germany is regarded as heavily overbanked with more than 3,600 commercial, public and cooperative banks battling for market share, and one branch per 1,100 inhabitants.
The top five, led by Deutsche, command a combined market share of just 14 percent and are struggling to make their cost-laden retail branch networks more efficient.
Their return on equity, lower than 10 percent after tax in most cases, is well below British, U.S. and Dutch banks -- too low to keep shareholders happy.
One of several merger scenarios is that Deutsche could join forces with Vereinsbank while Dresdner could link up with Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG.
The moves could make strategic sense as Deutsche and Dresdner are strong in investment banking while Vereinsbank and Hypo-Bank lean to mortgage banking.
Also, insurer Allianz AG Holding, which owns stakes of 22 percent each in Dresdner and Hypo-Bank, may put pressure on the two banks to get together, analysts added.
